confidence_note: Verified in a full text of the book (introduction and 'The Quickening'). Old text's 'wrong mountain', 'career restructuring', 'thinned friendships in 2013', 'NYT columnist at the summit' and 'the transition mostly comes after a break' are not supported in that form and were dropped; Brooks says the second mountain does not reject the first. Only the divorce in the summer of 2013 and his own first-mountain description are used as personal facts.
facts: Brooks describes a two-mountain shape of life: on the first mountain people establish an identity, cultivate talents, build a secure ego and try to make a mark; they keep score ('How do I measure up? Where do I rank?').
Its goals are the ones the culture endorses: to be a success, well thought of, invited into the right circles, personally happy.

Some reach the top and find it unsatisfying ('Is this all there is?'); others are knocked off by failure or by something unexpected such as a death, a cancer scare or an addiction; they end up 'in the valley'.

Brooks about himself: 'My first mountain was an insanely lucky one. I achieved far more professional success than I ever expected to.' But the climb made him 'aloof, invulnerable, and uncommunicative' and he 'sidestepped the responsibilities of relationship'.

He names his failures as 'failures of omission' and 'the sins of withdrawal: evasion, workaholism, conflict avoidance'; he says he was too busy, too distant for two old friends who live 250 miles away.

'Then came the events of the summer of 2013... My divorce happened. I was lonely, humiliated, adrift. I had a constant physical sensation of burning in my stomach and gut.' He and his ex-wife agreed not to discuss the marriage and divorce in public.
In seasons of suffering 'you have a tendency to grip the steering wheel tighter... but sometimes you get defeated and just let go of the wheel. Strange things begin happening.'

'The second mountain is not the opposite of the first mountain. To climb it doesn't mean rejecting the first mountain. It's the journey after it.' The test: where is your ultimate appeal, to self or to something outside of self?

First mountain: building up the ego, acquisition, ambitious, strategic, independent. Second mountain: shedding the ego, contribution, relational, intimate, relentless. 'You conquer your first mountain... You are conquered by your second mountain.'
scene_details: a constant burning sensation in the stomach
gripping the steering wheel tighter, then letting go
keeping score: 'How do I measure up?'
tension: A man whose first climb went far better than he expected describes it as the thing that made him aloof, and a divorce that did not fit the plan.
opening_idea: Open on 'an insanely lucky' first mountain and what it did to him, before the divorce.

lessons.idea: Ask where your ultimate appeal lies, to yourself or to something outside you; the second mountain adds a direction, it does not erase the first.
lessons.anchor: Brooks's own list of failures of omission, such as the friends 250 miles away.
lessons.example: A shop owner who is proud of the business notices she has not visited a friend in years and puts one visit in the diary.

reflect_final: Where in your life do you keep score, and where is the person or cause outside yourself that you keep too busy to show up for?

use_cases.situation: You catch yourself comparing your title with a peer's.
use_cases.move: Ask whether you are keeping score, as Brooks says first-mountain people do, and name one thing you could give someone this week.

use_cases.situation: A friend has hit a wall after a big success.
use_cases.move: Ask what the success did not give them; Brooks says some find the top unsatisfying and wonder 'Is this all there is?'.

use_cases.situation: A colleague you rarely call is going through something.
use_cases.move: Call, without an agenda; Brooks lists failures of omission, being too busy to show up, among his own.

pocket_idea: Brooks's failures were omissions, not scandals: the friends he was too busy to call. Name one you owe a call.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Brooks calls his first mountain insanely lucky, and says its lasting damage was being too busy for the people he loved.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Brooks's first career climb went better than he hoped, but it left him aloof; the summer of 2013 brought his divorce, and the second mountain is what he calls the journey after the first.
